sources.title: Foresight Without Seeing: Latent Futures for World Action Models

synopsis: ForeWAM gives a direct robot policy hidden predictive context through one Video DiT prefill, then reuses its K/V cache while an Action DiT denoises executable actions. A frozen teacher shapes dynamics registers only during training. Reported success is 96.7% on standard LIBERO and 61.6% on the observed LIBERO-Plus subset; Flash trades some subset robustness for lower latency. These are benchmark control results, with explicit coverage limits (e3, e5, e6, e9–e11).

problem.text: Generating future video can expose scene evolution to a policy but adds iterative inference cost. ForeWAM asks whether a direct action policy can access predictive dynamics through hidden features while dispensing with future-video generation. Its intended contribution is the combination of a distributed cache and compact, transition-supervised registers.

contributions.text: Future-KV constructs an action-facing interface over the current observation and stochastic future slots, caching video features once per action query.

Latent-action supervision is intended to make dynamics registers emphasize interaction-induced change. The paper evaluates the combined configuration, but does not establish that individual registers encode contact or are causally necessary.

inputs: Two synchronized camera views, language instruction and 8D proprioception (e3, e14).
Training additionally uses demonstrated future frames, executable actions and frozen-teacher transition targets (e6, e7).
outputs: A horizon-32 chunk of 7D executable actions: 6-DoF end-effector pose plus gripper control; no future video is generated at deployment (e5, e14).

steps.name: Encode observation and instruction
steps.detail: Concatenate two 224×224 camera views into a 224×448 image before VAE encoding. Use Wan2.1 text embeddings and project proprioception into a context token. Video and action branches have separate transformer stacks.

steps.name: Build hidden predictive context
steps.detail: Keep the current visual latent clean, append Gaussian future slots, and prefill the Video DiT once. Cache layer-wise keys and values and retain dynamics-register states. These hidden features are not decoded future observations.

steps.name: Route information into action denoising
steps.detail: Figure 3 shows current tokens reading current tokens, registers reading current/register tokens, and future tokens using causal temporal access. Action queries read all video/register groups and action tokens. In particular, registers do not read future slots under the depicted mask.

steps.name: Shape the compact interface
steps.detail: During training, a frozen inverse-dynamics teacher encodes a demonstrated visual transition. Mean-pool the dynamics registers and project them toward its latent target. The teacher supplies a non-executable learning target; the Action DiT supplies motor commands.

training.text: Initialize the visual branch from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and the action expert from a linearly interpolated Wan2.1 ActionDiT checkpoint. Both have 30 blocks, with widths 1536 and 1024. Use 16 dynamics registers and a 32D teacher target. No reported variant receives embodied pretraining before LIBERO training; the video initialization is still pretrained.

Each example contains 33 observation frames; temporal ratio four maps the 32-step action chunk to nine video frames. Joint training combines future-latent flow, action flow and register matching. AdamW uses learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 0.01, cosine annealing and clipping at 1.0; the flow schedule has 1,000 timesteps and shift 5.0.

inference.text: From the current observation, instruction and proprioception, prefill at sigma = 1.0 and reuse that cache for ten action-denoising steps. Flash uses OneDP distillation to reduce the action schedule to two steps while retaining the interface. Neither observed future frames nor teacher outputs are available.

The output is a control chunk, not a video plan requiring an inverse-dynamics decoder. The paper describes chunk-level queries but leaves the executed prefix length and exact observation-refresh cadence unspecified.

equations.explanation: Eqs. (3)–(4): o is the observation, l the instruction and p proprioception. The substrate concatenates the current latent with future-slot noise. D_theta is the dynamics-register slice; H_KV contains the per-layer cache. T indexes the visual sequence.
Eqs. (6)–(8): y is a demonstrated video latent or action chunk, epsilon is sampled noise, t is the flow time and f_theta predicts velocity. The target is epsilon minus y.

Eqs. (9)–(10): g_psi projects the mean of N_D registers D_i toward teacher target z_LA. sg stops teacher-target gradients; it does not detach the video-to-action interface. Lambda_LA weights register supervision; its numerical value is not specified.

results.setting: Spatial, Object, Goal and Long; 50 rollouts per task; no embodied pretraining for ForeWAM variants.
results.value: ForeWAM 96.7 overall; Flash 96.9. ForeWAM suite rates: 97.0, 99.6, 97.2, 92.8.
results.comparison: Fast-WAM 97.6 overall; ForeWAM and Flash are 0.9 and 0.7 percentage points lower.
results.interpretation: Flash preserves aggregate standard-suite performance in the reported runs. The table reports 2B parameters for either variant versus 6B for Fast-WAM; this is not a controlled size comparison.

results.setting: Observed subset spanning seven perturbation categories; external baseline results come from different sources.
results.comparison: Fast-WAM 51.5: differences are +10.1 and +6.7 percentage points. pi0.5 reports 85.7 overall.
results.interpretation: ForeWAM exceeds Fast-WAM in camera (62.5 versus 16.4) and noise (58.8 versus 37.7), but trails it in robot-initial-state shifts (37.4 versus 44.5) and lighting (74.1 versus 78.2). Gains are descriptive and not universal.

results.setting: One NVIDIA A800 GPU with 80 GB memory; ten action steps for ForeWAM, two for Flash.
results.comparison: Fast-WAM 667; Flash has about 61% lower latency than ForeWAM.
results.interpretation: The measurement concerns action generation, not task-completion time, achieved control frequency or physical-robot throughput.

results.setting: Three component configurations each have 1,482 coverage-matched observed evaluations; the base has 10,027 with different coverage.
results.value: Both components 61.6; Future-KV only 58.5; LA supervision only 58.0.
results.comparison: Combined configuration gains 3.1 and 3.6 percentage points over the single-component configurations. Base policy 53.6 is contextual.
results.interpretation: This supports configuration-level complementarity. A fully matched two-by-two experiment and causal interventions are still needed; subtracting the base row would confound coverage.

limitations.text: All evaluated control is confined to LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. Real-world transfer, other robot morphologies and broader long-horizon dynamics remain unverified.

Neither the mask nor aggregate success establishes that hidden future features represent accurate dynamics. Tables provide no uncertainty intervals, and external robustness baselines are not coverage-matched causal controls.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the specified Wan components, action initialization, frozen latent-action teacher and synchronized LIBERO trajectories. Main text calls the teacher LaWM while Appendix A says LaWAM; the exact checkpoint and action-initialization procedure need clarification.

Missing details include the latent-action loss weight, batch size, training steps, training hardware/time, software versions, exact LIBERO-Plus evaluation IDs/seeds and Flash distillation settings. The A800 specification describes inference only. These gaps prevent treating the appendix as a complete executable recipe.

reasoning.text: The separate Video DiT and Action DiT support Dual-system. However, IDM describes the frozen training teacher, not deployed action extraction: ForeWAM directly denoises executable actions from cached features. Therefore Q4/Dual-system × IDM is misleading as an inference-paradigm label. Joint training also does not make this a single shared model or joint future/action generation at deployment.

discussionQuestions: Would the register advantage persist with identical subset coverage and several training seeds (e12)?
Does intervention on future-slot K/V impair transition-sensitive tasks beyond the effect of removing generic context (e4–e7)?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author/affiliation block and arXiv version margin
evidence.detail: The title and six authors match the catalog after name-order normalization. The margin identifies arXiv:2608.11605v1 [cs.AI], 12 Aug 2026. Affiliations are Shanghai Jiao Tong University, ACE Robotics and Nanyang Technological University.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–3, Abstract and Section 1; p. 2, Figure 1 and caption
evidence.detail: The authors contrast cascaded, joint and direct-policy WAMs, and propose exposing hidden predictive context without future-video generation. ForeWAM-Flash uses OneDP to reduce action-denoising steps; no embodied robot-data pretraining is used.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Figure 2 and caption, Section 3.1, Eqs. (1)–(5)
evidence.detail: The policy conditions on observation, language and proprioception. At deployment a clean current latent is concatenated with Gaussian future slots; a single video prefill returns dynamics-register states and layer-wise K/V context for direct action prediction.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2, Token groups and routing; p. 6, Figure 3 and following paragraph
evidence.detail: The mask depicts current-frame, dynamics-register, future and action groups. Reading rows as queries, current tokens read current tokens; registers read current/register tokens; future rows add temporal access; action rows read all groups. Action queries concatenate cached video K/V with current action K/V.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.2, Future-KV prefill and inference paragraph
evidence.detail: At inference the video branch runs once at sigma = 1.0, retaining the clean current latent and filling future positions with pure noise. Per-layer K/V tensors are reused during action denoising; action-loss gradients remain connected to the prefill during training.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Latent-action-supervised dynamics registers; p. 7, Eq. (9) and following paragraph
evidence.detail: A frozen inverse-dynamics latent-action teacher produces a quantized, non-executable transition target. A trainable projection of mean-pooled dynamics registers matches it; stop-gradient applies only to the teacher target. The teacher is absent at deployment.

Video and action branches use continuous flow matching with interpolation (1-t)y+t epsilon and target velocity epsilon-y. The total loss sums video flow, action flow and weighted latent-action register matching. This objective alone does not prove causal necessity of the registers.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 4.1, Benchmarks and evaluation protocol
evidence.detail: Standard LIBERO uses Spatial, Object, Goal and Long suites with 50 rollouts per task. LIBERO-Plus perturbs viewpoint, robot initial state, language, lighting, background texture, sensor noise and object layout.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 1, ForeWAM, ForeWAM-Flash and Fast-WAM rows; Section 4.2
evidence.detail: Standard LIBERO overall success is 96.7% for ForeWAM and 96.9% for Flash versus 97.6% for Fast-WAM. ForeWAM's Spatial/Object/Goal/Long rates are 97.0/99.6/97.2/92.8%; Flash's are 97.8/99.2/97.4/93.0%. Both variants have 2B parameters versus Fast-WAM's 6B; all three show no embodied pretraining.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 2, Ours, Ours-Flash, Fast-WAM and pi0.5 rows; p. 7, Robustness on LIBERO-Plus
evidence.detail: On the observed subset, overall success is 61.6/58.2/51.5% for Ours/Flash/Fast-WAM. Camera success is 62.5/57.9/16.4%; noise is 58.8/53.7/37.7%; robot is 37.4/40.4/44.5%; light is 74.1/71.0/78.2%. The pi0.5 row reports 85.7% overall. External results have different sources, limiting causal comparison.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Section 4.3; p. 8, Table 3, all rows
evidence.detail: Standalone action-generation latency on one NVIDIA A800 80 GB GPU is 667 ms for Fast-WAM, 568 ms for Ours and 220 ms for Flash. ForeWAM uses ten action steps; Flash uses two. These measurements are not task-completion times or rollout statistics.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 4.4 and Table 4, all configurations
evidence.detail: Both components yield 61.6%, Future-KV only 58.5% and LA supervision only 58.0%, each over 1,482 coverage-matched observed evaluations. The base policy reports 53.6% over 10,027 evaluations with different coverage and is explicitly contextual.

Evaluation is restricted to LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. Different morphologies, broader tasks and real-world deployment remain unverified. The authors restrict robustness conclusions to the evaluated subset.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Appendix A, Architecture and inputs
evidence.detail: The visual branch retains Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B's Video DiT, text encoder and VAE; instruction embeddings are precomputed. Both transformer branches have 30 blocks, with widths 1536 and 1024. The action expert starts from a linearly interpolated Wan2.1 ActionDiT checkpoint. H=32; 33 observation frames map to nine video frames at temporal ratio four; two 224-by-224 views are concatenated to 224-by-448. Proprioception is 8D and actions are 7D.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Appendix A, Optimization and inference; p. 7, Eq. (10)
evidence.detail: The configuration uses 16 dynamics registers, a 32D frozen LaWAM teacher target, no readability registers, a 1,000-timestep flow schedule shifted by 5.0 and AdamW with learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 0.01, cosine annealing and clipping at 1.0. No batch size, training duration/hardware count, software versions or numerical latent-action loss weight is supplied here.
